strengths: Well-motivated and clearly scoped research question: mechanistic analysis of how VLMs resolve conflicts between visual input and parametric knowledge, a relatively underexplored area compared to unimodal knowledge-conflict studies.

The analysis goes beyond behavioral evaluation to causal claims: head identification via Logit Lens is validated with targeted multiplicative interventions on attention weights, and specificity is confirmed with a random-head control experiment (Fig. 9).

Patch attribution claims are causally validated by ablating identified visual tokens and comparing against both gradient-based and random ablation baselines (Fig. 5), supporting the claim that attention-based attribution is more precise.

Findings are replicated across two architecturally different models (LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b), with consistent qualitative patterns reported in appendices, strengthening confidence in the observations.

The WHOOPS-AHA! dataset construction process is documented, including the exact GPT-4o prompts in the appendix, with manual verification of factual/counterfactual token distinctions, and the paper is transparent about dataset filtering (436/432 usable examples).
Honest limitations section acknowledging Logit Lens distortions, single-token simplification, restriction to final-token attention, and synthetic nature of the data.
Intervention side effects are monitored (rank shifts in the token distribution, KL divergence, caption quality degradation at high |λ|), and the choice of 20 heads is empirically justified (Fig. 10).
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to prior work: the core methodology closely extends Ortu et al. (2024) from text-only LLMs to VLMs, and concurrent work (Golovanevsky et al., 2025a) already steers modality competition in VLMs; the main differentiator (complex counterfactual scenes from WHOOPS!) is a dataset design choice rather than a new method.

Only two models are analyzed, both in a narrow size range; generalization of the 'attention favors visual context, MLPs favor internal knowledge' dichotomy to other VLM families (e.g., models with different visual encoders or cross-attention architectures) remains untested.

Dataset construction depends on GPT-4o for generating sentences and token sets; the manual verification procedure is not quantified (how many annotators, agreement rates), and GPT-4o's own knowledge biases could correlate with or against the studied models' parametric knowledge in unexamined ways.

Reliance on Logit Lens as the primary identification tool is a known-fragile diagnostic (as the authors concede); no complementary technique such as tuned lens, path patching, or activation patching is used to corroborate head roles.

Interventions are relatively blunt (post-softmax multiplicative scaling of attention at only the final token position), which may introduce distributional artifacts; while rank shifts and KL divergence are reported, a cleaner causal validation (e.g., activation patching) is absent.

Comparison to gradient-based attribution covers only one gradient method; no comparison to modern saliency or attention-free attribution baselines (e.g., integrated gradients variants, attention rollout, or perturbation-based methods), weakening the 'outperforms gradient-based attribution' claim.

The image-region analysis uses first-token prediction only, and the paper acknowledges it does not analyze full generations; the extent to which findings hold for open-ended multimodal reasoning is unknown.
Statistical rigor is limited: some figures include error bars but no significance tests are reported for key comparisons (e.g., 61% vs 29% image attention, head-group differences).
Several methodological parameters (20 heads, τ thresholds, λ range) are chosen empirically without systematic sensitivity analysis in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored question: the internal mechanisms by which VLMs resolve conflicts between visual input and parametric knowledge, extending a previously textual-only interpretability framework (Ortu et al., 2024) to the multimodal setting.

The methodology combines complementary forms of evidence: observational localization via logit inspection, causal validation via targeted attention-head interventions with a random-head control, and spatial localization via patch ablation with a random-patch control. The inclusion of controls strengthens the causal claims.
The results are replicated on two architecturally different models (LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b), with consistent qualitative trends, which improves confidence in the findings beyond a single model.

The WHOOPS-AHA! dataset construction is described in detail (GPT-4o prompts provided in Appendix D, manual verification of factual/counterfactual token sets), and the filtering of ambiguous cases is reported.

The paper is generally clearly written and well organized, with an honest Limitations section that acknowledges the known distortions of Logit Lens, the single-token simplification, and the restricted scope of the interventions.
A reproducibility statement is provided (hardware, software, compute time), and the dataset builds on a CC-BY licensed resource.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely an incremental extension of existing work: the analytical pipeline directly mirrors Ortu et al. (2024), and the concurrent Golovanevsky et al. (2025a) work covers closely related territory (steering model predictions in multimodal knowledge-prior conflicts). The differentiation (complex counterfactual scenes vs. simple attribute edits) is real but modest.

Heavy reliance on Logit Lens as the primary diagnostic, a technique the authors themselves concede introduces systematic distortions from non-final residual states; no complementary probing method (e.g., tuned lens) is used to validate the localization results.

The headline claim that attention-based attribution 'outperforms gradient-based attribution in precision' is supported only indirectly by ablation curves; no precision/recall-style metric against ground-truth counterfactual regions is computed, and the qualitative evidence (Figure 6) rests on only two cherry-picked examples.

Key experimental choices are somewhat ad hoc: the selection of exactly 20 heads per group is justified post hoc via an incremental-improvement curve, and the intervention operates post-softmax at a single token position, with measurable side effects (factual token rank drifting from 3 to 31), limiting the strength of the steering claim.

The dataset is small and derived from a single source (~500 WHOOPS! images, ~430 usable per model), generated by GPT-4o; the scope of generalization to naturalistic conflicts or a broader model population (only two VLMs) is limited.

The evaluation is restricted to single-token logit comparisons between one factual and one counterfactual token per example, which simplifies the generative behavior considerably and weakens claims about 'conflict resolution' in full generation.

The 'Code and Dataset' footnote in the paper appears to contain no actual link, which is a reproducibility concern; without released code and data, full verification of the pipeline is not currently possible.

The practical payoff is limited: the intervention recovers factual accuracy to ~74-83% from a low baseline but does not establish robust control of free-form generation, and the authors explicitly position the work as diagnostic rather than deployable.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: how VLMs resolve conflicts between visual input and internal parametric knowledge, an area where most prior work is behavioral/benchmark-only (as the related-work section credibly establishes).

A coherent analysis pipeline with proper causal validation: Logit Lens localization of factual vs. counterfactual heads is followed by targeted attention interventions (Eqs. 4-5), and a random-head control experiment (Fig. 9) confirms the effects are specific to the identified heads rather than an artifact of attention perturbation.

The patch-ablation analysis (Sec. 4.4) provides an additional, independent line of causal evidence, with a random-patch control and qualitative examples (Fig. 6) showing that highlighted regions align with semantically meaningful anomalous content.

Reproducibility is addressed directly (Sec. 3.4): public models and implementations, modest compute (15 GPU-hours), dataset license stated, and full dataset-generation prompts provided in Appendix D, making the pipeline reconstructable.
Findings replicate across two architecturally different models (LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b), which strengthens the generality of the localization claims.

Honest limitations section: the authors acknowledge the distortions of Logit Lens (citing Belrose et al.), the single-token simplification, and the restriction to attention heads at the final token position.
Concurrent work (Golovanevsky et al., 2025a) is transparently disclosed and the differentiation (complex commonsense-violating scenes vs. simple attribute edits) is well argued.
weaknesses: The core methodology is a direct adaptation of Ortu et al. (2024) from text-only LMs to VLMs; the technical novelty is moderate, and the paper's contribution rests mainly on the new setting and dataset rather than new analysis tools.

The analysis is confined to a single factual/counterfactual token at the final prompt position; behavior over full generations, where hallucination actually manifests, is not analyzed, limiting the ecological validity of the 'knowledge conflict resolution' claims.

Reliance on Logit Lens is a known-weak diagnostic (the authors concede this), and no complementary technique (e.g., tuned lens, patching at intermediate positions, or activation patching) is used to triangulate the head-localization findings.

Dataset construction depends on GPT-4o generation with manual verification, but no inter-annotator agreement, verification protocol details, or dataset statistics/quality metrics are reported; potential noise or overlap between Sfact and Scofa candidate sets is not quantified.

Key hyperparameters appear somewhat post hoc: the choice of 20 heads is justified by a diminishing-returns curve (Fig. 10), and the intervention range λ ∈ [-3,3] is partly justified by downstream generation quality, both chosen without pre-registered criteria.

The claim that attention-based attribution outperforms gradient-based attribution in 'precision' rests on a single ablation-curve comparison (Fig. 5); no other standard baselines (e.g., occlusion/saliency maps, attention rollout, Grad-CAM variants) are included, so the comparative claim is under-supported.
The dataset/code release footnote is an empty placeholder in the manuscript, which prevents full verification of reproducibility claims at review time.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the main quantitative results (e.g., the 61% vs. 29% attention gap, intervention effects), despite the dataset being reasonably large (~436 examples).

The mechanistic story (attention transmits counterfactual signal directly to the final token in late layers) is plausible but the causal chain is only indirectly probed; direct path-level patching would be needed to firmly support the 'limited intermediate processing' conclusion.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: how VLMs resolve conflicts between parametric commonsense knowledge and conflicting visual evidence, extending the text-only 'competition of mechanisms' line of work (Ortu et al., 2024) to the multimodal setting.

Careful dataset construction (WHOOPS-AHA!) with an explicit requirements analysis, GPT-4o generation pipeline, dual LLM-as-a-judge validation, and human validation with both exact and adjacent agreement reported; construction prompts are fully disclosed in the appendix.

Strong causal methodology: head identification via logit lens, targeted bidirectional attention interventions with dose-response curves, a random-head control experiment, a variable-number-of-heads analysis, and an MLP-intervention control showing attention-specific effects.

Comprehensive alternative-explanation checks: POPE evaluation showing the identified counterfactual heads are not generic vision heads (no degradation on routine visual grounding), and replication on the independently constructed Visual CounterFact dataset with substantial head overlap, supporting transferability of the mechanism.

Quantitative attribution comparison (attention vs. gradient vs. random, with SAM-3 ground-truth masks, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, median/IQR reporting) substantiates the claim that conflict heads act as precise visual pointers.

Honest, detailed limitations section covering logit-lens approximation errors, final-token-position focus, and the restriction to late-fusion architectures; reproducibility appendix documents compute and setup, and code/data release is promised.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core pipeline (logit-lens head ranking plus attention interventions on conflict tokens) directly mirrors Ortu et al. (2024) in the text-only setting, and concurrent VLM work (Golovanevsky et al. 2025a/b, Hua et al. 2025) already studies modality preference and head-level conflict effects; the delta is the implicit-commonsense setting and the attribution-byproduct finding.

Coverage is limited to two late-fusion models; the paper's own limitations concede generalizability to other fusion strategies is unknown, and the central claim about a 'general mechanism' rests on just two architectures from overlapping design families.

Analysis is confined to single representative factual/counterfactual tokens at the final token position; free-form generation behavior is only assessed anecdotally (caption-quality table and KL divergence), so the mechanism's role in realistic generative outputs is under-verified.

The intervention (post-softmax multiplicative rescaling of the last attention row) is a fairly blunt instrument; while random-head controls mitigate this, the paper does not fully rule out that the intervention's effect stems from the number of heads touched or general disruption of late-layer processing, given 40 targeted heads vs. 100 random ones in the control.

Human validation is thin: 20 items and 2 evaluators, with exact agreement as low as 35% for text-only alignment (salvaged only by adjacent-category agreement), leaving dataset quality partially dependent on LLM judges.

Small effect-scope issues: dataset shrinks to ~435 examples after filtering, attribution analysis uses only 20 sampled images, and there are minor internal inconsistencies (e.g., 61% vs. 60% attention-to-image figures between text and Figure 3); the finding that 'attention favors visual context, MLPs favor knowledge' is broadly consistent with prior expectations, reducing surprise value.

strengths: Technically sound methodology: the identification pipeline (logit lens → head ranking → attention-weight intervention) is accompanied by multiple well-designed controls, including intervention on 100 randomly selected heads (Fig. 11), ablation of random patches (Fig. 5), MLP-intervention controls (Appendix C), and a POPE control showing the identified heads are conflict-specific rather than generic vision heads (Appendix H). These controls meaningfully strengthen the causal claims.

Consistency across two architectures (LLaVA-NeXT-7B, Gemma3-12B) and replication of the full identification/intervention procedure on an independent dataset (Visual CounterFact, Appendix G), including reported head overlap (13-14/20 counterfactual heads shared), supports the claim of a transferable mechanism.

The attribution comparison is quantified rather than only qualitative: SAM-3-derived ground-truth masks, an object-vs-background ratio metric, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and comparison against gradient and random-head baselines (Table 4).

WHOOPS-AHA! is a reusable resource: the construction pipeline, prompts, LLM-as-a-judge validation, and human validation on a subset are documented in appendices, and code/dataset are released. Reproducibility details (hardware, 20 GPU hours, library versions) are provided.
Clear writing and honest limitations section that acknowledges Logit Lens approximation errors, the single-token simplification, and the late-fusion-only scope.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The central findings — a small set of late-layer attention heads resolving parametric-vs-contextual competition, attention favoring context while MLPs favor parametric knowledge — closely mirror Ortu et al. (2024) in the text-only setting and overlapping VLM results in Golovanevsky et al. (2025a,b) and Hua et al. (2025). The paper's differentiation (implicit commonsense conflicts, head-recruitment specificity) is real but modest; the contribution is largely an adaptation of an existing methodology to a new modality.

Dataset scale and generality are limited: only ~436/432 usable examples after filtering, each reduced to a single-word completion with one representative factual and counterfactual token. This constrains the ecological validity of claims about 'conflict resolution' in richer generation settings, which the authors concede but which weakens the practical impact of both the dataset and the mechanism analysis.

Dataset quality assurance is partly circular: completions generated by GPT-4o and validated primarily by LLM judges (GPT-4.1, Gemini), with human validation on only 20 items by 2 evaluators and moderate exact agreement (35-65% exact on alignment).

The headline attribution comparison (Section 5.4 / Appendix I) rests on only 20 sampled images, limiting the statistical strength of the claim that head attention outperforms gradient attribution; the LLaVA-NeXT effect over gradients (2.05 vs 1.88) is comparatively small.

Analysis is confined to two late-fusion models and the final-token position; generalization to earlier-fusion architectures and full free-form generation is left to future work, so the scope of the mechanistic claims is narrower than the framing suggests.

Minor presentation issues: an internal inconsistency in the counterfactual-head image-attention figure (60% in the caption vs 61% in text vs 52% for Gemma3 in Fig. 9), and reliance on Logit Lens despite the authors' acknowledgment of its known distortions (tuned lens would have been a stronger choice).

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly scoped question: how do VLMs resolve conflicts between parametric commonsense knowledge and contradictory visual evidence, with a mechanistic (rather than purely behavioral) analysis that is still rare for multimodal models.

WHOOPS-AHA! is a useful, reusable resource: it builds on the established WHOOPS! benchmark, includes paired factual/counterfactual token sets enabling token-level analysis, and is validated with both LLM-as-a-judge (two judges, agreement rates reported) and human evaluation, with prompts and rubrics fully disclosed in the appendix.

The causal claims are supported by an unusually thorough set of controls: intervention on randomly selected heads (Fig. 11), a sweep over the number of intervened heads (Fig. 10), an MLP-intervention comparison (Appendix C), a POPE control showing the identified heads are not generic vision-processing components (Table 3), KL-divergence analysis justifying the intervention strength range, and replication on an independent dataset (Visual CounterFact) with substantial head overlap (Appendix G).
Results replicate across two architecturally different models (LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B), strengthening the claim that late-layer attention heads mediate the conflict.

The attribution contribution (Section 5.4, Appendix I) goes beyond qualitative examples: it uses SAM-derived ground-truth masks, a quantitative Average Ratio metric, statistical testing (Wilcoxon), and comparison against both gradient-based and random-head baselines.

Honest limitations section that correctly identifies Logit Lens approximation errors, the single-token simplification, and the restriction to late-fusion architectures. Reproducibility details (compute, libraries, licenses) are provided, and code/data release is promised.
weaknesses: The entire identification pipeline depends on Logit Lens, which the authors themselves acknowledge is an approximate, potentially distorted diagnostic; an analysis with tuned lens or activation patching as a complementary validation is missing, leaving some uncertainty about whether the identified heads are genuinely causally special or partly artifacts of the probe.

The single-token framing (one t_fact and one t_cofa per example) substantially simplifies the phenomenon; the paper does not demonstrate that the findings transfer to free-form generation beyond the qualitative caption examples, which limits the practical significance of the 'steering' claim.

The choice of exactly 20 heads per group is justified post hoc as an 'optimal balance' (Fig. 10), which is somewhat circular: the number is selected on the same data used to report the main intervention results, and no held-out validation is performed.

Dataset construction relies on GPT-4o for both prompts and token sets, and the judge models are GPT-4.1/Gemini; there is a risk of circularity or contamination (e.g., GPT-4o-designed prompts that align with GPT-family world knowledge), and human validation covers only 20 items with modest exact agreement (35–60% for some dimensions).

The comparison with gradient-based attribution, while favorable to the authors' method, uses a fairly standard gradient baseline and only 20 sampled images for the quantitative evaluation (Appendix I); the sample size is small, and stronger baselines from the saliency/attribution literature are not considered.

Head-identity overlap between datasets (13/20, 14/20) is reported as evidence of transferability, but the headline framing of 'a small set of heads' could have been more carefully quantified (e.g., how much of the intervention effect the overlapping subset alone accounts for).
Factual accuracy under intervention plateaus around 74–83% rather than returning to text-only baselines, indicating the intervention is partial; the paper does not analyze the residual gap.
